abstract: Autonomous ML agents in large organizations exchange data and model outputs across organizational and legal boundaries. Which rules bind a given exchange is not fixed. It depends on where the data subjects live, where the agents run, who owns them, whom they target, and which version of each rule is in force. Tags that describe the data can be noisy, and a counterparty can overclaim its safeguards. We model one exchange as a \emph{regime-uncertain transfer game} between two ML agents, with an enforcer as a third player. Rules enter as hard constraints with a strictest-wins structure. Agents hold a Bayesian belief over which rules apply, can pay to unlock safeguards or verify claims, and then bargain over the remaining legal bundles.Our method, Legally-Constrained Nash Bargaining (\LCNB), implements this with a Monotonic Concession Protocol using Zeuthen's rule. We prove four properties of the model and test it in a synthetic simulator with GDPR, DPDP, CCPA/CPRA and a stylised stricter regime. In two of three stress cases where residence and citizenship differ, a citizenship-based rule violates in 21--37\% of shared records, and \LCNB{} in under 1\%. The results also show limits. With our default economics, \LCNB{} shares almost only aggregates, and its low violation rate follows partly from that. Violation tolerance, tag noise and enforcement strength matter more than the choice of bargaining solution.
summary: Autonomous ML agents in large organizations exchange data and model outputs across organizational and legal boundaries. Which rules bind a given exchange is not fixed.
title: Regime-Uncertain Data Transactions: A Game-Theoretic Framework for Self-Adapting and Self-Diagnosing Multi-ML-Agent Systems
